doc.title: Chico Hamilton interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 30, 2000

title: Where he fits among drummers
summary: No two drummers play alike; he names Max, Kenny Clarke, Jo Jones, Buddy Rich and others, and Rowe comments on influence.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why

blocks.x: And active I guess. If you can be real honest, and don’t worry about your ego, can you tell me where do you fit in the line of drummers in innovation and in your music? I mean I don’t know if I asked that question very well but—

Well I don’t know. I’m being very honest. First of all it’s totally impossible for two drummers to play alike, because of the physical aspect. One might have long arms, one might have short arms. And if you have short arms that means that you have to sit closer to your instrument. If you have long arms you sit back, that type of thing, for reach. And just the space between makes a difference in the sound you’re going to get, or the touch you’re going to acquire to get the sound. I don’t sound like anybody else, and I don’t know of anybody who sounds like me. Here again, it becomes very personal. It all depends on what you like and what you don’t like. You see, I think that anybody, drummers, that try to play, is doing a hell of a job, is contributing to something. So the old adage about “hey give the drummer some” that’s the bottom line. But I don’t know, I just do what I do. And Louis Hayes does what he does, Max does what he does, Kenny Clarke did what he did, Jo Jones did what he did, Sonny Greer. All of them. Elvin Hayes, Buddy Rich, Gene Krupa. They’re all — that’s how broad and beautiful this whole thing is in regards to playing or approaching that instrument. So it all depends on whose beat you dig.
It’s usually left to the non-musicians I guess to try to put down, this guy was influenced by this guy, influenced by this guy, and so forth. Sometimes it’s true and sometimes maybe not.
